scenario.title: Resident-level bootstrap manufactures precision
scenario.trap: Resampling residents treats 1,200 nested observations as 1,200 experiments and returns a confidence interval several times too narrow.
scenario.truth: The design supplies 20 independent worlds. The true mean loss difference is +0.6.
scenario.defence: Resample whole worlds; residents travel with the world they belong to.

naive.analysis: iid bootstrap over residents, both arms independent

findings.detail: The correct interval is 3.9x wider. The naive analysis claims 1200 independent units where the design supplies 20.

findings.finding: the understatement shows up as under-coverage
findings.detail: Over 60 independent replications of the whole experiment, the nominal-95% resident-level interval covered the true difference 62% of the time; the world-level interval covered it 90% of the time.

lines: records: 2400 observations in 20 worlds (60 observations per world per policy)
true mean loss difference (B - A): +0.600
WRONG  resident-level bootstrap: +1.161 [+0.902, +1.421]  width 0.519
RIGHT  world-level paired bootstrap: +1.161 [+0.192, +2.205]  width 2.013
width ratio (right / wrong): 3.9x
measured coverage over 60 replications -- resident: 62%, world: 90% (nominal 95%)
design effect for policy_a: 1.9 (ICC 0.88, 40 observations worth 21 independent ones)

scenario.title: World-level bootstrap is calibrated
scenario.trap: A single interval proves nothing; calibration has to be measured over repeated experiments.
scenario.truth: The true mean loss difference is +0.6 in every replication.
scenario.defence: Measure coverage: a nominal 95% interval should contain the truth about 95% of the time.

findings.finding: world-level cluster bootstrap is approximately calibrated
findings.detail: Across 100 replications the nominal-95% world-level interval covered the true difference 90% of the time at 20 worlds and 98% at 60 worlds. The percentile bootstrap under-covers slightly when clusters are few, which is why the validator warns below 20 clusters rather than staying silent -- but it is calibrated in a way the resident-level interval never becomes, at any number of residents.

findings.finding: more residents per world cannot fix a resident-level interval
findings.detail: The resident-level interval narrows as residents are added while its coverage stays broken, because the missing variance is between worlds. Only more worlds buy precision that is real.

lines: true mean loss difference (B - A): +0.600
world-level paired interval on this draw: [+0.192, +2.205] -> covers the truth
measured coverage over 100 replications at 20 worlds: 90% (nominal 95%)
measured coverage over 50 replications at 60 worlds: 98% (nominal 95%)
for contrast, resident-level coverage: 61%
mean interval width -- world: 1.723, resident: 0.659

scenario.title: Mean favours A while tail risk favours B
scenario.trap: policy_a has the lower average loss, so a mean-only report recommends it.
scenario.truth: policy_a carries a 4% per-observation chance of a +60 loss; its 90% CVaR is far worse than policy_b's while its mean is 0.8 better.
scenario.defence: Declare tail metrics up front and report the disagreement rather than resolving it silently.

truth.design: policy_a shifts loss down by 3.2 but carries a 4% chance of a +60 catastrophe per observation, worth +2.4 on average -- a net mean advantage of 0.8 bought with a heavy tail

naive.conclusion_if_reported_alone: mean_loss: policy_a beats policy_b. The 95% paired interval for policy_b - policy_a is (0.3655, 1.332) and excludes 0.

disagreements.message: TAIL DISAGREEMENT on `loss`: mean_loss favours policy_a while cvar90_loss favours policy_b. Average performance and tail risk point in opposite directions; reporting either alone would mislead.

METRIC SPLIT for policy_b vs policy_a: different declared metrics resolve in favour of different policies (mean_loss->policy_a, cvar90_loss->policy_b, success_rate->policy_a). There is no single winner; the choice depends on which metric the decision actually cares about, and that must be declared in advance.

findings.finding: mean and tail resolve in opposite directions
findings.detail: Reporting either statistic alone yields a confident and opposite recommendation. The disagreement is the result, and the decision needs a pre-declared risk preference to resolve it.

lines: mean_loss   B - A = +0.846 [+0.365, +1.332] -> favours policy_a
cvar90_loss B - A = -2.709 [-4.710, -1.216] -> favours policy_b
TAIL DISAGREEMENT on `loss`: mean_loss favours policy_a while cvar90_loss favours policy_b. Average performance and tail risk point in opposite directions; reporting either alone would mislead.

METRIC SPLIT for policy_b vs policy_a: different declared metrics resolve in favour of different policies (mean_loss->policy_a, cvar90_loss->policy_b, success_rate->policy_a). There is no single winner; the choice depends on which metric the decision actually cares about, and that must be declared in advance.

scenario.title: Practically equivalent, and provably so
scenario.trap: The interval includes zero, so the report says 'no significant difference' and readers hear 'the same'.
scenario.truth: The true difference is +0.03 against a practical margin of 0.40 -- real, and negligible.
scenario.defence: TOST against the declared margin turns 'we failed to detect' into 'we established equivalence'.

truth.design: a real but negligible difference, with enough worlds to resolve it

naive.analysis: declare 'no difference' because the interval includes zero
naive.why_wrong: An interval that includes zero is consistent with zero and with every other value it contains. Without a margin it cannot distinguish 'the same' from 'we did not look hard enough'.

correct.analysis: TOST against a declared practical margin
correct.interpretation: Equivalent within +/-0.4: the 90% interval for the difference (-0.09097, 0.08149) lies entirely inside the declared practical margin.

findings.finding: equivalence requires a margin, and with one it is concludable
findings.detail: Equivalent within +/-0.4: the 90% interval for the difference (-0.09097, 0.08149) lies entirely inside the declared practical margin.

lines: true difference: +0.030, declared practical margin: +/-0.4
paired difference: -0.0055 [-0.1068, +0.0970]  (bootstrap p = 0.885)
WRONG  'p > 0.05, therefore the policies are the same.'
RIGHT  Equivalent within +/-0.4: the 90% interval for the difference (-0.09097, 0.08149) lies entirely inside the declared practical margin.
verdict: equivalent -- mean_loss: policy_b and policy_a are practically equivalent within +/-0.4. The interval (-0.09097, 0.08149) fits inside the margin.

scenario.title: Missing worlds reverse the ranking
scenario.trap: policy_b has no results on the 22 hardest worlds; comparing each policy over its own worlds makes the worse policy look better.
scenario.truth: policy_b is worse by +1.2 mean loss on every world.
scenario.defence: Pair on the worlds both policies ran, and record every world excluded.

truth.design: policy_b has no results on the 22 hardest worlds -- the pattern produced by runs that crash, time out, or are quietly excluded

naive.analysis: compare each policy over whatever worlds it has

correct.analysis: paired comparison restricted to worlds both policies ran

findings.finding: the missing worlds, not the policies, drive the unpaired ranking
findings.detail: policy_b is absent from the 22 hardest worlds. Comparing each policy over its own world set credits policy_b with the easy material it happened to be given.

lines: true difference (B - A): +1.200 (positive = B is worse)
policy_b is missing from 22 of 60 worlds -- the hardest ones
WRONG  unpaired over available worlds: -1.862 [-3.147, -0.770] -> favours policy_b
RIGHT  paired on the 38 shared worlds: +0.948 [+0.622, +1.266] -> favours policy_a
The ranking reverses. Nothing about either policy changed; only which worlds were counted.

scenario.title: A policy wins only because it was tested on easier worlds
scenario.trap: policy_a was run mostly on flat worlds and policy_b mostly on steep ones; pooling the two makes policy_a look better.
scenario.truth: policy_b is better by -1.5 mean loss on identical worlds.
scenario.defence: Pair on shared worlds, print the allocation ledger, and report per stratum.

truth.design: policy_a ran on 30 flat worlds and 6 steep; policy_b on 30 steep and 6 flat. Only 12 worlds carry both.

naive.analysis: pool every world each policy ran and compare the means

correct.analysis: paired on shared worlds, plus the allocation ledger and per-stratum results

findings.finding: allocation, not policy quality, drives the pooled ranking
findings.detail: The allocation table shows the policies were run on different terrain in different proportions. Pairing on the shared worlds and reporting per stratum both recover the true direction.

lines: true difference (B - A): -1.500 (negative = B is better)
allocation: policy_a ran on 30 flat worlds and 6 steep; policy_b on 30 steep and 6 flat. Only 12 worlds carry both.
WRONG  pooled over each policy's own worlds: +3.223 [+2.137, +4.479] -> favours policy_a
RIGHT  paired on the 12 shared worlds: -1.693 [-2.053, -1.371] -> favours policy_b
allocation imbalance on `landscape`: 67% share gap
stratum flat: favours policy_b
stratum steep: favours policy_b
